properties.name: Kingdom of Prussia (Frederick the Great)
properties.group: Built schooling for obedience and uniformity
properties.what they did: Its 1763 General School Regulation (Generallandschulreglement) required all children, girls and boys, to be schooled from 5 to 13 or 14; critics argue the system was built for obedience, social control and loyalty to the state.

properties.name: Horace Mann (Massachusetts Board of Education)
properties.group: Built schooling for obedience and uniformity
properties.what they did: Travelled to Prussia in 1843 to study its schools and on his return championed tax-supported common schools and teacher training in Massachusetts, a model copied across the United States (he warned against Prussia's obedience to the authorities).

properties.name: General Education Board (Rockefeller)
properties.group: Private money steering what schools teach
properties.what they did: Rockefeller's board, incorporated by Congress in 1903, shaped schooling across the American South; its Occasional Papers No. 1 (1913) by Frederick T. Gates: "In our dream, we have limitless resources and the people yield themselves with perfect docility to our molding hand."

properties.name: Carnegie Foundation for the Advancement of Teaching
properties.group: Tests and standards that rank and sort children
properties.what they did: Made the Carnegie Unit - 120 hours of class time per course - the standard for American high schools, by offering professors' pensions only to colleges that adopted it; near-universal by 1910.
properties.placed at: New York City, where it was founded

properties.name: Carlisle Indian Industrial School (Richard Henry Pratt)
properties.group: Used schooling to erase peoples' cultures
properties.what they did: Founded 1879 by Pratt, whose motto was "Kill the Indian, save the man": over 7,800 children from 140 Native nations had their hair cut, languages banned and names changed, 1879-1918. The model for US Indian boarding schools.

properties.name: Government of Canada (Department of Indian Affairs) and the churches
properties.group: Used schooling to erase peoples' cultures
properties.what they did: Funded and ran, with Christian churches, the residential schools about 150,000 Indigenous children were made to attend; the Truth and Reconciliation Commission found they amounted to cultural genocide.

properties.name: College Board (the SAT)
properties.group: Tests and standards that rank and sort children
properties.what they did: Owns, develops and publishes the SAT, the admissions test first given in 1926.

properties.name: Educational Testing Service
properties.group: Tests and standards that rank and sort children
properties.what they did: Administers the SAT; in 2015 took over most of Texas's state testing from Pearson.

properties.name: Pearson
properties.group: Tests and standards that rank and sort children
properties.what they did: Held Texas's state testing contract for 2010-2015, nearly half a billion dollars ($88.3 million for 2012-13 alone); also helped fund the Common Core standards.

properties.name: Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation
properties.group: Private money steering what schools teach
properties.what they did: Spent more than $200 million to develop and promote the Common Core standards, funding policy groups, unions, the US Chamber of Commerce and messaging firms (Washington Post, 2014); also an investor in Bridge International Academies.

properties.name: National Governors Association and Council of Chief State School Officers
properties.group: Tests and standards that rank and sort children
properties.what they did: Created the Common Core State Standards, convening their writers in late 2008.

properties.name: Walton Family Foundation
properties.group: Private money steering what schools teach
properties.what they did: Pledged $1 billion over five years from 2016 for schools, and $250 million for charter school buildings (the Building Equity Initiative).

properties.name: Whittle Communications (Channel One News)
properties.group: Selling to children through schools
properties.what they did: From 1989 gave schools televisions and satellite dishes in exchange for showing its daily news, with two minutes of advertising, to students; about eight million American teenagers watched in 1997-2000.

properties.name: The Coca-Cola Company
properties.group: Selling to children through schools
properties.what they did: Signed exclusive school drink contracts; Colorado Springs' district got $8 million over 10 years with its 53 schools expected to sell 70,000 cases a year (Education Week, 1998).

properties.name: PepsiCo
properties.group: Selling to children through schools
properties.what they did: Signed exclusive school drink contracts, among them $2.1 million over 7 years with Jefferson County, Colorado, and $1.95 million over 5 years with Hurst-Euless-Bedford, Texas (Education Week, 1998).

properties.name: Google (Google for Education)
properties.group: Selling to children through schools
properties.what they did: The Electronic Frontier Foundation's complaint to the US Federal Trade Commission (1 December 2015) said school Chromebooks let Google collect every site students visit, every search, the videos they watch and their saved passwords, without asking students or parents.

properties.name: Junior Achievement
properties.group: Selling to children through schools
properties.what they did: Founded 1919 by Horace A. Moses, AT&T's Theodore Vail and Winthrop M. Crane; brings business, work-readiness and entrepreneurship lessons into schools, about ten million students a year.

properties.name: Bridge International Academies
properties.group: Private money steering what schools teach
properties.what they did: Runs for-profit primary schools in Kenya, Uganda, Nigeria, India and Liberia (about 750,000 pupils in 2022) where teachers read scripted lessons from tablets; backed by the Gates Foundation, the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative and the World Bank's IFC; Uganda's High Court ruled in 2016 that its schools ran without proper licences.

properties.name: OECD (PISA)
properties.group: Tests and standards that rank and sort children
properties.what they did: Tests 15-year-olds in 91 countries and ranks them; Germany's "PISA shock" led every German state to adopt common national standards; scholars question whether the data can bear the policy decisions built on them.

properties.name: Cambridge International Education (Cambridge Assessment, University of Cambridge)
properties.group: Tests and standards that rank and sort children
properties.what they did: Its exams (Cambridge IGCSE, International AS and A Levels) are taught in over 10,000 schools in more than 160 countries, to nearly two million students a year.

properties.name: International Baccalaureate
properties.group: Tests and standards that rank and sort children
properties.what they did: Its programmes ran in 6,234 schools in more than 160 countries and territories on 1 September 2022; the United States has the most.

properties.name: McGraw Hill
properties.group: Textbook and test publishers and the investment firms that own them
properties.what they did: Sold by Apollo's funds to Platinum Equity for $4.5 billion in 2021; listed on the New York Stock Exchange in July 2025, with Platinum still its largest shareholder. Since June 2025 it builds Pearson's PRoPL tests into its K-12 courses (a partnership, not a merger).

properties.name: Houghton Mifflin Harcourt (HMH)
properties.group: Textbook and test publishers and the investment firms that own them
properties.what they did: Taken private by Veritas Capital for about $2.8 billion in April 2022; bought NWEA, maker of the MAP Growth tests, in May 2023, and says it reaches over 50 million students. In 2007 analysts estimated that Houghton Mifflin, Harcourt, Pearson and McGraw-Hill together made 80 to 85 per cent of US K-12 textbook sales.

properties.name: Cengage Group
properties.group: Textbook and test publishers and the investment firms that own them
properties.what they did: Textbook and online course publisher, controlled by Apax Partners since Apax and OMERS bought it for $7.75 billion in 2007; Apollo's funds put $500 million into it in 2023.

properties.name: Apollo Global Management
properties.group: Textbook and test publishers and the investment firms that own them
properties.what they did: Bought McGraw-Hill Education for $2.4 billion in 2013 (sold it on in 2021); led the $1.14 billion purchase of Apollo Education Group, owner of the University of Phoenix, in 2017; put $500 million into Cengage in 2023.
properties.placed at: head office, 9 West 57th Street, New York

properties.name: KKR
properties.group: Textbook and test publishers and the investment firms that own them
properties.what they did: With Dragoneer, bought Instructure, maker of the Canvas learning system used by schools and universities, in November 2024, valuing it at about $4.8 billion.
properties.placed at: head office, 30 Hudson Yards, New York

properties.name: Blackstone
properties.group: Textbook and test publishers and the investment firms that own them
properties.what they did: Made a large investment in Renaissance Learning in 2021, a K-12 testing and software company that says it is in more than 40 per cent of US schools.
properties.placed at: head office, 345 Park Avenue, New York

properties.name: Veritas Capital
properties.group: Textbook and test publishers and the investment firms that own them
properties.what they did: Owns Houghton Mifflin Harcourt (taken private for about $2.8 billion in 2022) and, through it, NWEA's MAP Growth tests (2023).

properties.name: Microsoft
properties.group: Tech and AI companies moving into classrooms
properties.what they did: Lead funder ($12.5 million of $23 million) of the American Federation of Teachers' National Academy for AI Instruction (2025); one of the more than 60 first signers of the White House pledge on AI in schools (June 2025).

properties.name: OpenAI
properties.group: Tech and AI companies moving into classrooms
properties.what they did: Put $10 million into the American Federation of Teachers' National Academy for AI Instruction (2025), with Microsoft and Anthropic.

properties.name: Apple
properties.group: Tech and AI companies moving into classrooms
properties.what they did: One of the more than 60 first signers of the White House 'Pledge to America's Youth: Investing in AI Education' (30 June 2025), which commits signers to funding, lessons and training for schools over four years.

properties.name: Amazon
properties.group: Tech and AI companies moving into classrooms
properties.what they did: One of the more than 60 first signers of the White House 'Pledge to America's Youth: Investing in AI Education' (30 June 2025).

properties.name: UNESCO (Global Education Coalition)
properties.group: Global bodies opening schooling to business
properties.what they did: Set up its Global Education Coalition in March 2020, as schools closed for COVID, with Microsoft, Google, Facebook, Zoom, KPMG, Coursera and others as members supplying technology.
properties.placed at: head office, place de Fontenoy, Paris

properties.name: Global Partnership for Education
properties.group: Global bodies opening schooling to business
properties.what they did: Counts Cisco, Google, Microsoft, Vodacom, Econet Wireless, Ecobank and Standard Bank as partners, with business represented on its board. A 2023 Transnational Institute report argues that such arrangements lead to privatisation and a 'democratic deficit'.

properties.name: Harvard University
properties.group: Elite universities that train the ruling class
properties.what they did: Endowment of $56.9 billion (fiscal 2025). Said in 2021 it would make no new direct investments in fossil fuel companies, letting its older holdings run off.

properties.name: Yale University
properties.group: Elite universities that train the ruling class
properties.what they did: Endowment of $44.1 billion (30 June 2025). Has not divested from fossil fuels as a whole: it leaves out a list of companies (mostly coal and climate misinformation) and stays invested in others.

properties.name: University of Oxford
properties.group: Elite universities that train the ruling class
properties.what they did: Educated 31 UK prime ministers, 13 of them at Christ Church.

properties.name: University of Cambridge
properties.group: Elite universities that train the ruling class
properties.what they did: Educated 15 UK prime ministers, six of them at Trinity College.

properties.name: Sciences Po
properties.group: Elite universities that train the ruling class
properties.what they did: Six presidents of France's Fifth Republic studied there: Pompidou, Mitterrand, Chirac, Sarkozy, Hollande and Macron.

properties.name: ÉNA (École nationale d'administration), now INSP
properties.group: Elite universities that train the ruling class
properties.what they did: Trained four French presidents (Giscard d'Estaing, Chirac, Hollande, Macron) and eight prime ministers. Abolished at the end of 2021 and replaced on 1 January 2022 by the Institut national du service public.

properties.name: Corinthian Colleges
properties.group: Degrees sold, not earned: predatory colleges and diploma mills
properties.what they did: For-profit college chain that closed in 2015 after actions over falsified job placement rates; in 2022 the US government cancelled $5.8 billion of its 560,000 former students' loans.

properties.name: University of Phoenix
properties.group: Degrees sold, not earned: predatory colleges and diploma mills
properties.what they did: Paid a record $191 million FTC settlement in 2019 ($50 million in cash and $141 million of student debt cancelled) over ads falsely claiming job partnerships with Microsoft, AT&T, Twitter and others. Owned from 2017 by a group led by Apollo's funds.

properties.name: Trump University
properties.group: Degrees sold, not earned: predatory colleges and diploma mills
properties.what they did: Settled the fraud lawsuits brought by its former students for $25 million (agreed 2016, final 2018).

properties.name: Axact
properties.group: Degrees sold, not earned: predatory colleges and diploma mills
properties.what they did: Ran at least 370 websites for fake universities and accreditors, taking money from over 215,000 people in 197 countries (New York Times investigation, 2015).
